trace.question: According to Attention Is All You Need, how is scaled dot-product attention computed?
trace.answer:
Scaled dot‑product attention is computed as follows:

1. Compute the dot product of each query with all keys.  
2. Divide each dot‑product by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) (the square root of the key dimension).  
3. Apply a softmax to the scaled scores to obtain attention weights.  
4. Multiply the weights by the values and sum to produce the output.

Mathematically, for query matrix \(Q\), key matrix \(K\), and value matrix \(V\),

\[
\text{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V .
\]

[1706.03762v7, PDF p. 4]

trace.question: According to Attention Is All You Need, how is scaled dot-product attention computed?
trace.answer:
Scaled dot‑product attention is computed as  

\[
\text{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V ,
\]

where \(Q\) (queries), \(K\) (keys) and \(V\) (values) are matrices whose columns are the respective vectors, and \(d_k\) is the dimensionality of the key (and query) vectors. The dot products are divided by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) before the softmax to prevent large values from pushing the softmax into regions with very small gradients.  

[1706.03762v7, PDF p. 4]

To this end, we add "positional encodings" to the input embeddings at the bottoms of the encoder and decoder stacks. The positional encodings have the same dimension dmodel as the embeddings, so that the two can be summed. There are many choices of positional encodings, learned and fixed [9]. In this work, we use sine and cosine functions of different frequencies: PE(pos,2i) = sin(pos/100002i/dmodel) PE(pos,2i+1) = cos(pos/100002i/dmodel) where pos is the position and i is the dimension. That is, each dimension of the positional encoding corresponds to a sinusoid. The wavelengths form a geometric progression from 2π to 10000 · 2π. We chose this function because we hypothesized it would allow the model to easily learn to attend by relative positions, since for any fixed offset k, PEpos+k can be represented as a linear function of PEpos. We also experimented with using learned positional embeddings [9] instead, and found that the two versions produced nearly identical results (see Table 3 row (E)). Another is the amount of computation that can be parallelized, as measured by the minimum number of sequential operations required. One key factor affecting the ability to learn such dependencies is the length of the paths forward and backward signals have to traverse in the network. This mimics the typical encoder-decoder attention mechanisms in sequence-to-sequence models such as [38, 2, 9]. • The encoder contains self-attention layers. In a self-attention layer all of the keys, values and queries come from the same place, in this case, the output of the previous layer in the encoder. Each position in the encoder can attend to all positions in the previous layer of the encoder. • Similarly, self-attention layers in the decoder allow each position in the decoder to attend to all positions in the decoder up to and including that position. We need to prevent leftward information flow in the decoder to preserve the auto-regressive property. trace.question: Why does Attention Is All You Need use positional encodings?
trace.answer:
The Transformer has no recurrence or convolution, so the model has no inherent sense of the order of tokens in a sequence.  
To give the network information about the relative or absolute positions of tokens, the authors add **positional encodings** to the input embeddings at the bottoms of both the encoder and decoder stacks. These encodings have the same dimensionality as the embeddings so they can be summed directly. The paper notes that the sinusoidal form was chosen because it allows the model to learn to attend by relative positions and may enable extrapolation to longer sequences than seen during training.  

> “Since our model contains no recurrence and no convolution, in order for the model to make use of the order of the sequence, we must inject some information about the relative or absolute position of the tokens in the sequence. To this end, we add 'positional encodings' to the input embeddings … We chose the sinusoidal version because it may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than the ones encountered during training.”  
> [1706.03762v7, PDF p. 6]

(right) Multi-Head Attention consists of several attention layers running in parallel. of the values, where the weight assigned to each value is computed by a compatibility function of the query with the corresponding key. 3.2.1 Scaled Dot-Product Attention We call our particular attention "Scaled Dot-Product Attention" (Figure 2). The input consists of queries and keys of dimension dk, and values of dimension dv. We compute the dot products of the query with all keys, divide each by √dk, and apply a softmax function to obtain the weights on the values. In practice, we compute the attention function on a set of queries simultaneously, packed together into a matrix Q. The keys and values are also packed together into matrices K and V . We compute the matrix of outputs as: Attention(Q, K, V ) = softmax(QKT )V (1) √dk The two most commonly used attention functions are additive attention [2], and dot-product (multi- plicative) attention. Dot-product attention is identical to our algorithm, except for the scaling factor of √dk1 . Additive attention computes the compatibility function using a feed-forward network with a single hidden layer. While the two are similar in theoretical complexity, dot-product attention is much faster and more space-efficient in practice, since it can be implemented using highly optimized matrix multiplication code. While for small values of dk the two mechanisms perform similarly, additive attention outperforms dot product attention without scaling for larger values of dk [3].

trace.question: How does multi-head attention work in Attention Is All You Need?
trace.answer:
Multi‑head attention is a way of running several scaled dot‑product attention mechanisms in parallel and then combining their outputs.  
For each head \(i\) the input query, key and value matrices \((Q,K,V)\) are linearly projected with learned weight matrices \(W_i^Q, W_i^K, W_i^V\) to lower‑dimensional spaces of size \(d_k\) and \(d_v\).  
The attention for that head is then computed as  

\[
\text{head}_i = \text{Attention}\!\left(QW_i^Q,\; KW_i^K,\; VW_i^V\right)
= \operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{(QW_i^Q)(KW_i^K)^{\!\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) VW_i^V
\]

[1706.03762v7, PDF p. 4]  

The outputs of all \(h\) heads are concatenated and projected once more with a final weight matrix \(W^O\) to produce the final multi‑head attention output:

\[
\text{MultiHead}(Q,K,V)=\operatorname{Concat}(\text{head}_1,\dots,\text{head}_h)W^O
\]

[1706.03762v7, PDF p. 5]  

In the Transformer the authors use \(h=8\) heads, each with \(d_k=d_v=d_{\text{model}}/h=64\). Because each head operates on a reduced dimensionality, the overall computational cost is comparable to a single‑head attention with full dimensionality, while allowing the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions.  

Thus, multi‑head attention works by projecting the inputs into several subspaces, applying scaled dot‑product attention independently in each subspace, and then concatenating and projecting the results back to the model dimension.

trace.question: How does multi-head attention work in Attention Is All You Need?
trace.answer:
**Multi‑head attention in the Transformer**

1. **Linear projections**  
   Each head receives its own linear projections of the input vectors.  
   For a head \(i\) the queries, keys and values are projected with learned matrices  
   \(W_i^Q \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_k}\),  
   \(W_i^K \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_k}\) and  
   \(W_i^V \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_v}\).  
   The projections reduce the dimensionality of each head to \(d_k=d_v=d_{\text{model}}/h\) (here \(h=8\), \(d_{\text{model}}=512\), so \(d_k=d_v=64\)).  
   [1706.03762v7, PDF p. 5]

2. **Scaled dot‑product attention per head**  
   For each head the attention is computed as  
   \[
   \text{Attention}(Q_i,K_i,V_i)=\text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{Q_iK_i^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V_i .
   \]
   The scaling by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) prevents large dot‑products from pushing the softmax into regions with very small gradients.  
   [1706.03762v7, PDF p. 4]

3. **Parallel execution**  
   All \(h\) heads compute their attention outputs in parallel, producing \(h\) vectors of dimension \(d_v\) for each position.  
   [1706.03762v7, PDF p. 5]

4. **Concatenation and final linear projection**  
   The outputs of the heads are concatenated and projected back to the model dimension with a learned matrix \(W^O \in \mathbb{R}^{h d_v \times d_{\text{model}}}\):
   \[
   \text{MultiHead}(Q,K,V)=\text{Concat}(\text{head}_1,\dots,\text{head}_h)W^O .
   \]
   This yields the final multi‑head attention output of dimension \(d_{\text{model}}\).  
   [1706.03762v7, PDF p. 5]

5. **Purpose**  
   By attending in multiple sub‑spaces simultaneously, the model can capture different types of relationships (e.g., syntactic, semantic) that would be averaged out if only a single attention head were used.  
   [1706.03762v7, PDF p. 5]

Thus, multi‑head attention consists of projecting queries, keys and values into several lower‑dimensional spaces, applying scaled dot‑product attention independently in each space, concatenating the results, and projecting back to the original dimensionality.

1 Introduction Recurrent neural networks, long short-term memory [13] and gated recurrent [7] neural networks in particular, have been firmly established as state of the art approaches in sequence modeling and transduction problems such as language modeling and machine translation [35, 2, 5]. Numerous efforts have since continued to push the boundaries of recurrent language models and encoder-decoder architectures [38, 24, 15]. Recurrent models typically factor computation along the symbol positions of the input and output sequences. Aligning the positions to steps in computation time, they generate a sequence of hidden states ht, as a function of the previous hidden state ht−1 and the input for position t. This inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples, which becomes critical at longer sequence lengths, as memory constraints limit batching across examples. Recent work has achieved significant improvements in computational efficiency through factorization tricks [21] and conditional computation [32], while also improving model performance in case of the latter. The fundamental constraint of sequential computation, however, remains. Attention mechanisms have become an integral part of compelling sequence modeling and transduc- tion models in various tasks, allowing modeling of dependencies without regard to their distance in the input or output sequences [2, 19]. In all but a few cases [27], however, such attention mechanisms are used in conjunction with a recurrent network. In this work we propose the Transformer, a model architecture eschewing recurrence and instead relying entirely on an attention mechanism to draw global dependencies between input and output. The Transformer allows for significantly more parallelization and can reach a new state of the art in translation quality after being trained for as little as twelve hours on eight P100 GPUs. 2 Background The goal of reducing sequential computation also forms the foundation of the Extended Neural GPU [16], ByteNet [18] and ConvS2S [9], all of which use convolutional neural networks as basic building block, computing hidden representations in parallel for all input and output positions. In these models, the number of operations required to relate signals from two arbitrary input or output positions grows in the distance between positions, linearly for ConvS2S and logarithmically for ByteNet. This makes it more difficult to learn dependencies between distant positions [12]. In the Transformer this is reduced to a constant number of operations, albeit at the cost of reduced effective resolution due to averaging attention-weighted positions, an effect we counteract with Multi-Head Attention as described in section 3.2. Self-attention, sometimes called intra-attention is an attention mechanism relating different positions of a single sequence in order to compute a representation of the sequence. Self-attention has been used successfully in a variety of tasks including reading comprehension, abstractive summarization, textual entailment and learning task-independent sentence representations [4, 27, 28, 22]. End-to-end memory networks are based on a recurrent attention mechanism instead of sequence- aligned recurrence and have been shown to perform well on simple-language question answering and language modeling tasks [34]. To the best of our knowledge, however, the Transformer is the first transduction model

trace.answer:
**Multi‑head attention in the Transformer**

The Transformer replaces the recurrent or convolutional layers with an attention‑only architecture.  
Instead of a single attention operation that uses the full model dimension \(d_{\text{model}}\), the model projects the queries, keys and values into several lower‑dimensional subspaces and runs the attention operation in parallel on each subspace. The results are then concatenated and linearly projected back to the model dimension.

Formally, for a set of queries \(Q\), keys \(K\) and values \(V\):

\[
\text{MultiHead}(Q,K,V)=
\Big[\text{head}_1,\dots ,\text{head}_h\Big]W^O
\]

where each head is computed as

\[
\text{head}_i=\text{Attention}\!\left(QW_i^Q,\; KW_i^K,\; VW_i^V\right)
\]

with learned projection matrices  
\(W_i^Q,W_i^K\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_k}\),  
\(W_i^V\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_v}\) and  
\(W^O\in\mathbb{R}^{h d_v\times d_{\text{model}}}\) [1706.03762v7, PDF p. 5].

In the original Transformer the authors use \(h=8\) heads, with \(d_k=d_v=d_{\text{model}}/h=64\). Because each head operates on a reduced dimension, the total computational cost is comparable to a single‑head attention with full dimensionality, but the model can attend to information from multiple representation subspaces simultaneously. This mitigates the averaging effect that would occur if only one attention head were used, allowing the network to capture richer, position‑specific dependencies across the sequence [1706.03762v7, PDF p. 5].

question: How does Moshi support full-duplex spoken dialogue?

evidence.text: Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue Figure 1: Overview of Moshi. Moshi is a speech-text foundation model which enables real-time spoken dialogue. The main components of Moshi’s architecture are: a bespoke text language model backbone (Helium, see Section 3.2); a neural audio codec with residual vector quantization and with semantic knowledge distilled from a self-supervised speech model (Mimi, Section 3.3); the streaming, hierarchical generation of semantic and acoustic tokens for both the user and Moshi, along with time-aligned text tokens for Moshi when using Inner Monologue (Section 3.4). been proposed by Wang et al. (2024), with an ASR system running in parallel to a text generator that feeds into a streaming TTS. While this allows modeling more complex sce- narios than previous approaches, it still relies on a cascaded pipeline and models both the user’s and the system’s speech into a single token stream, which is challenging in presence of significant overlap. The only previous full-duplex dialogue system is dGSLM (Nguyen et al., 2023), which models user and system speech as separate audio token streams and pro- poses a Siamese architecture to process both streams jointly. While dGSLM is full-duplex, it remains a proof-of-concept: it does not run in an online fashion, it does not benefit from the knowledge of a text language model, and it does not model acoustic information as it only models semantic tokens. Moshi addresses these limitations altogether: by modeling two streams of semantic and acoustic tokens hierarchically, Moshi is full duplex and can exploit all the information from the user (linguistic and non-linguistic) while producing speech in real time. Thanks to text pretraining and Inner Monologue, Moshi benefits from the knowledge of its Helium backbone. Finally, as the model produces acoustic tokens along with text and semantic tokens, it can generate an arbitrary range of emotions, voices and acoustic conditions. To the best of our knowledge, Moshi is the first audio language model that successfully addresses the many aforementioned challenges of spoken dialogue. 3 Model 3.1 Overview Moshi is a multi-stream speech-to-speech Transformer model, which allows for full-duplex spoken dialogue with a user thanks to an innovative architecture summarized in Figure 1. 6

Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue Alexandre D´efossez∗ alex@kyutai.org Laurent Mazar´e∗ Manu Orsini Am´elie Royer Patrick P´erez Herv´e J´egou Edouard Grave∗2024 Neil Zeghidour∗ neil@kyutai.org KyutaiSep ∗Equal contribution 17 Abstract We introduce Moshi, a speech-text foundation model and full-duplex spoken dialogue frame- work. Current systems for spoken dialogue rely on pipelines of independent components, namely voice activity detection, speech recognition, textual dialogue and text-to-speech. Such frameworks cannot emulate the experience of real conversations. First, their complex-[eess.AS] ity induces a latency of several seconds between interactions. Second, text being the inter- mediate modality for dialogue, non-linguistic information that modifies meaning— such as emotion or non-speech sounds— is lost in the interaction. Finally, they rely on a segmenta- tion into speaker turns, which does not take into account overlapping speech, interruptions and interjections. Moshi solves these independent issues altogether by casting spoken dia- logue as speech-to-speech generation. Starting from a text language model backbone, Moshi generates speech as tokens from the residual quantizer of a neural audio codec, while model- ing separately its own speech and that of the user into parallel streams. This allows for the removal of explicit speaker turns, and the modeling of arbitrary conversational dynamics. We moreover extend the hierarchical semantic-to-acoustic token generation of previous work to first predict time-aligned text tokens as a prefix to audio tokens. Not only this “Inner Monologue” method significantly improves the linguistic quality of generated speech, but we also illustrate how it can provide streaming speech recognition and text-to-speech. Our re- sulting model is the first real-time full-duplex spoken large language model, with a theoret- ical latency of 160ms, 200ms in practice, and is available at github.com/kyutai-labs/moshi.arXiv:2410.00037v1 Keywords: speech, text, multimodal, foundation, spoken dialogue 1

trace.question: How does Moshi support full-duplex spoken dialogue?
trace.answer:
Moshi achieves full‑duplex spoken dialogue by modelling the user’s and the system’s speech as **two parallel streams of semantic and acoustic tokens** that are generated and processed hierarchically.  
* The architecture is a multi‑stream speech‑to‑speech Transformer that can listen and speak simultaneously, removing the need for explicit speaker‑turn boundaries and allowing overlapping speech, interruptions, and interjections to be handled naturally.  
* By generating both semantic and acoustic tokens for each stream, Moshi preserves non‑linguistic information (e.g., emotion, prosody) that would otherwise be lost in a cascaded ASR‑TTS pipeline.  
* The model also uses an “Inner Monologue” method that prefixes time‑aligned text tokens to the audio tokens, improving linguistic quality while remaining compatible with streaming inference.  

These design choices give Moshi the first real‑time, full‑duplex spoken dialogue system with a theoretical latency of 160 ms and practical latency of ~200 ms.

While these models are trained in a supervised fashion with specific input and output sequences, Spirit-LM (Nguyen et al., 2024) uses tem- poral alignment between speech and its transcript to perform modality switch (from speech tokens to text tokens, or conversely) inside a sequence. Another approach, adopted by Spectron (Nachmani et al., 2024) and PSLM (Mitsui et al., 2024), combines speech and text in a hierarchical manner rather than as interchangeable representations. evidence.text: Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue Figure 2: Architecture and training of Mimi, our neural audio codec, with its split residual vector quantization. During training (blue part, top), we distill non- causal embeddings from WavLM (Chen et al., 2022) into a single vector quantizer which produces semantic tokens, and is combined with separate acoustic tokens for reconstruction. tion (Salimans and Kingma, 2016). All convolutions are causal, such that this autoencoder can run in a streaming fashion. With 4 convolutional blocks and respective striding fac- tors (4, 5, 6, 8), and a final 1D convolution with stride 2, Mimi’s encoder projects a 24kHz waveform to a latent representation of 12.5 frames per second and dimension D = 512. Symmetrically, the decoder adopts a similar structure but with transposed convolutions rather than strided ones, to project the latent representation back to 24kHz audio. We discretize the latent space with a Residual Vector Quantizer (Zeghidour et al., 2022), which iteratively applies vector quantization (VQ) to the residuals of the previous quantizer. With Q quantizers, each with a codebook of NA centroids, the RVQ discretizes the latent space into {1, . . . , NA}S×Q. As a baseline, we train this model with a combination of reconstruc- tion and adversarial losses, following the setup of Encodec (D´efossez et al., 2023). We detail below the main changes of Mimi with respect to this default configuration. Transformer-based bottleneck. To improve the ability of Mimi to encode speech into compact representations while reconstructing high-quality audio, we add Transformer mod- ules in the bottleneck, one right before quantization and one after. These Transformers have 8 layers, 8 heads, RoPE position encodings, a finite context of 250 frames (20 sec- onds), GELU (Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2016a) activations, a model dimension of 512 and an MLP dimension of 2048. To stabilize training, we use LayerScale (Touvron et al., 2021), with initialization of the diagonal values at 0.01. Both Transformers use causal masking, which preserves the compatibility of the whole architecture with streaming inference. Both Transformers prove to be useful with regard to perceived audio quality, while Transformer in the encoder also improves the distillation of semantic information described below (see Table 3 for ablation studies). Causality and streaming. With the mentioned hyper-parameters, Mimi is causal and can be used in a streaming fashion, both for encoding and decoding. Both its initial frame size and overall stride correspond to 80ms, meaning that given a first audio frame of 80ms, Mimi outputs a first latent timestep, which can be decoded to 80ms of output audio. 10

In addition, to capture the input user audio and output Moshi’s voice with high quality and in an efficient manner, we propose Mimi (Section 3.3), a neural audio codec combining semantic and acoustic information into a single tokenizer by using residual vector quantization and knowledge distillation. To jointly model the audio streams from Moshi and the user, as well as Moshi’s text tokens, we rely on a Depth Transformer compatible with streaming inference (Sections 3.4.1, 3.4.2). In this section, we further detail each of these components. We then describe the training datasets and the different training phases we used to train Moshi in Section 4. Mimi is the neural audio codec that Moshi uses to convert raw audio into discrete tokens and back again. It performs the following functions:

1. **Encoding audio into a compact latent representation** – Mimi’s encoder projects a 24 kHz waveform into a latent space of 12.5 frames s⁻¹ with dimension D = 512, using causal convolutions and a residual vector‑quantizer (RVQ) to discretize the latent space into semantic and acoustic tokens.  
   [2410.00037v1, PDF p. 10]

2. **Decoding tokens back to waveform** – The decoder, mirroring the encoder with transposed convolutions, reconstructs 24 kHz audio from the quantized latent representation.  
   [2410.00037v1, PDF p. 10]

3. **Providing both semantic and acoustic information to Moshi** – Mimi distills semantic knowledge from a self‑supervised speech model (WavLM) into the first level of acoustic tokens, enabling Moshi to generate intelligible speech without explicit text conditioning.  
   [2410.00037v1, PDF p. 3]

4. **Enabling streaming inference** – All convolutions in Mimi are causal, and its initial frame size and stride correspond to 80 ms, allowing the codec to operate in a streaming fashion for both encoding and decoding.

All convolutions are causal, such that this autoencoder can run in a streaming fashion. With 4 convolutional blocks and respective striding fac- tors (4, 5, 6, 8), and a final 1D convolution with stride 2, Mimi’s encoder projects a 24kHz waveform to a latent representation of 12.5 frames per second and dimension D = 512. Symmetrically, the decoder adopts a similar structure but with transposed convolutions rather than strided ones, to project the latent representation back to 24kHz audio. With Q quantizers, each with a codebook of NA centroids, the RVQ discretizes the latent space into {1, . . . , NA}S×Q. trace.question: How does Moshi use semantic and acoustic tokens?
trace.answer:
Moshi models speech and text as a single joint sequence of **semantic tokens** (representing the linguistic content) and **acoustic tokens** (representing the waveform).  
* The model generates **semantic and acoustic tokens jointly** rather than first producing all semantic tokens and then generating acoustics. This joint generation enables **streaming modeling** of both modalities at the same time[2410.00037v1, PDF p. 14].  
* In the joint sequence, each step \(V_{s,k}\) contains a semantic token and an acoustic token. The acoustic tokens are delayed by a fixed acoustic delay \(\tau\) (e.g., \(\tau = 2\) s) so that the acoustic stream can be aligned with the text stream while still allowing real‑time inference[2410.00037v1, PDF p. 56].  
* The Depth Transformer predicts tokens **from bottom to top**: acoustic tokens are kept to match the input audio, whereas semantic tokens are sampled freely. This design provides fine‑grained timestamps for words and supports both ASR and synthesis modes[2410.00037v1, PDF p. 56].

trace.question: How does Moshi use semantic and acoustic tokens?
trace.answer:
Moshi models dialogue as a joint sequence of **semantic** and **acoustic** tokens that are generated and consumed in a streaming fashion.  
* The first sub‑sequence of each step \(V_{s,k}\) is the **semantic** token \(A_{s,1}\) (the “semantic codebook” of the audio codec).  
* The remaining sub‑sequences \(A_{s,q}\) for \(q>1\) are **acoustic** tokens that encode the waveform.  
* An **acoustic delay** \(\tau\) is applied so that the acoustic tokens for step \(s\) are taken from the audio of step \(s-\tau\) (Eq. 4). This reduces the dependency between semantic and acoustic sub‑sequences and improves generation quality [2410.00037v1, PDF p. 14].  
* During inference the model samples tokens from the bottom (acoustic) to the top (semantic) of the depth transformer. Tokens above the dashed line (user side) are fed from the user, while tokens below (Moshi side) are sampled, allowing overlapping speech turns [2410.00037v1, PDF p. 15].  
* In text‑to‑speech mode the same joint sequence is used, but the text tokens are forced into the model and the acoustic tokens are generated with a 2‑second delay, providing fine alignment between words and audio [2410.00037v1, PDF p. 57].

trace.question: How does Moshi use semantic and acoustic tokens?
trace.answer:
Moshi models dialogue as a joint sequence of **semantic** and **acoustic** tokens that are generated (or conditioned on) by two transformer stacks: a Temporal Transformer that processes the whole sequence step‑by‑step, and a Depth Transformer that predicts the sub‑sequences for each step.

1. **Semantic tokens**  
   * The first sub‑sequence of each step, \(V_{s,1}\), contains the semantic information.  
   * In the audio‑only setting this sub‑sequence is produced by the first codebook of the Mimi audio codec, which encodes high‑level linguistic content (Section 3.3.2).  
   * When Moshi is used for text‑to‑speech (TTS) or for an inner‑monologue, a text stream \(W\) (obtained by SentencePiece tokenisation of a Whisper transcription) is inserted as the first sub‑sequence of \(V\). This acts as a prefix that conditions the generation of the semantic tokens, improving linguistic quality [2410.00037v1, PDF p. 15].

2. **Acoustic tokens**  
   * The remaining sub‑sequences, \(V_{s,q}\) for \(q>1\), encode acoustic features.  
   * They come from the other codebooks of the Mimi codec (12.5 steps s⁻¹, 8 codebooks).  
   * An **acoustic delay** \(\tau\) is applied: for step \(s\ge \tau+1\), the acoustic token \(V_{s,q}\) is set to the token from the user’s audio at step \(s-\tau\) (Equation 4). This reduces inter‑sub‑sequence dependencies and stabilises generation [2410.00037v1, PDF p. 14].

3. **Joint generation**  
   * At inference, the Depth Transformer samples tokens from bottom to top (semantic → acoustic).  
   * The Temporal Transformer receives the sum of the embeddings of the previous step’s tokens, allowing it to model the temporal dynamics across both semantic and acoustic streams.  
   * The acoustic delay lets the Temporal Transformer focus on modelling the inter‑dependence between semantic and acoustic tokens, while the Depth Transformer handles the intra‑step generation [2410.00037v1, PDF p. 15].

4. **Special modes**  
   * **TTS mode**: the text stream is delayed by 2 s and \(\tau=2\); acoustic tokens are sampled conditioned on the delayed text, giving fine word‑level alignment [2410.00037v1, PDF p. 57].  
   * **ASR mode**: the text stream is delayed by 2 s and \(\tau=2\); acoustic tokens are kept from the input audio, while text tokens are sampled freely, providing timestamps for words [2410.00037v1, PDF p. 56].

Thus, Moshi uses semantic tokens to represent linguistic content and acoustic tokens to represent waveform‑level details, synchronising them with a controlled delay to achieve stable, high‑quality real‑time dialogue generation.

trace.question: What is the inner-monologue mechanism described in Moshi?
trace.answer:
**Inner‑Monologue in Moshi**

Inner‑Monologue is a training and inference strategy that lets Moshi generate a *textual* representation of its own speech before producing the corresponding semantic and acoustic tokens.  
- During training, Moshi first predicts a sequence of text tokens \(W\) (obtained by tokenising the Whisper transcription of its own audio) and uses this text as a prefix for the subsequent prediction of semantic tokens.  
- The text stream is inserted as the first sub‑sequence in the joint sequence \(V\) that the model conditions on, so that the semantic and acoustic predictions are conditioned on the already‑generated text.  
- At inference time, the model samples tokens from the Moshi stream (semantic, text, acoustic) while the user stream tokens are fed from the user. The text tokens are generated first, then the semantic tokens, and finally the acoustic tokens, all within the same Transformer pass.  

This hierarchical, per‑frame generation (text → semantic → acoustic) provides a scaffolding that improves linguistic quality and spoken fluency without significantly increasing inference cost. The effect is evident in the ablation studies, where enabling Inner‑Monologue yields a large boost in speech intelligibility and spoken question‑answering accuracy.

trace.question: What is the inner-monologue mechanism described in Moshi?
trace.answer:
**Inner‑Monologue in Moshi**

Inner‑Monologue is a training and architectural component that lets Moshi generate a *textual* representation of its own speech before producing the corresponding acoustic tokens.  
- The model first predicts a sequence of text tokens (derived from a SentencePiece tokenizer applied to a Whisper transcription of the audio it will produce).  
- These text tokens are inserted as a prefix in the joint sequence that the model learns to generate, so that the subsequent semantic and acoustic tokens are conditioned on the text.  
- This hierarchical, per‑frame generation (text → semantic → acoustic) keeps the overall sequence length unchanged while providing a linguistic scaffold that improves the quality and intelligibility of the generated speech.  
- In practice, enabling Inner‑Monologue increases spoken‑question‑answering accuracy by almost a factor of three and only adds a negligible inference cost (one extra token per timestep) [2410.00037v1, PDF p. 15] and [2410.00037v1, PDF p. 29].

trace.question: What is the inner-monologue mechanism described in Moshi?
trace.answer:
The **Inner‑Monologue** component in Moshi is a hierarchical generative mechanism that jointly models text, semantic, and acoustic tokens. It decomposes a spoken utterance into a chain of these token types and predicts them in a hierarchical, multi‑stream fashion. Unlike prior approaches that switch between modalities or generate a full text sequence before producing audio, Inner‑Monologue predicts each token type in parallel while keeping the overall sequence length manageable for the Transformer. This design allows Moshi to generate speech in real‑time, support arbitrary voices and conditions, and derive streaming TTS and ASR systems from the same model.  

- Inner‑Monologue decomposes speech into a chain of text, semantic, and acoustic tokens and predicts this structured sequence hierarchically, enabling representation of all utterances as both text and speech without modality switching.  
- It predicts on a per‑frame basis, so each prediction step outputs a speech frame, making Moshi compatible with real‑time generation.  
- The hierarchical modeling (Section 3.4.4) allows decomposing the generation task without increasing the Transformer’s sequence length, unlike Chain‑of‑Modality.  
- When combined with a delay between token types, Inner‑Monologue enables streaming TTS and ASR systems derived from Moshi.

evidence.text: • Direct byte-level language modeling with isotropic architectures3 can be improved with efficient sequence models such as MambaByte (Wang et al. 2024), but still incur prohibitive computational costs while underperforming tokenized models in compute-matched settings. • To improve efficiency, hierarchical architectures such as Hourglass Transformer (Nawrot, Tworkowski, et al. 2022) and MegaByte (Yu, Simig, et al. 2023) use small byte-level models to compress raw inputs into subsampled sequences, which are then processed with a more powerful standard language model. However, simple pooling strategies such as compressing every 𝑘inputs are not data-dependent, and perform poorly on modalities with variable information rates such as language. • SpaceByte (Slagle 2024) and Byte Latent Transformer (Pagnoni et al. 2024) introduce data-dependent chunking strategies such as delimiter- or entropy-based heuristics. These heuristics, however, rely on auxiliary external boundary predictors, and are therefore modality-specific and not fully end-to-end. • Although jointly trainable boundary predictors are the ideal solution, they require optimizing discrete selection operations without supervision, which is fundamentally a challenging problem. Consequently, existing end-to-end approaches (Nawrot, Chorowski, et al. 2023) exhibit training instabilities that preclude scaling beyond small models or nesting multi-level hierarchies. Fundamentally, creating a tokenizer-free architecture requires incorporating the data chunking process directly into the model, while overcoming challenges in efficiency, learnability, and stability at scale. Dynamic Chunking: End-to-end Sequence Modeling Without Tokenization In this work, we introduce an end-to-end hierarchical network (H-Net) that compresses raw data through a recursive, data-dependent dynamic chunking (DC) process (Figure 1). H-Nets match the efficiency of tokenized pipelines while substantially improving modeling ability, by replacing handcrafted heuristics with content-aware and context-dependent segmentation learned from data. Hierarchical Processing. The H-Net adopts the hierarchical architecture from prior work (Goel et al. 2022; Nawrot, Tworkowski, et al. 2022; Slagle 2024), resembling an autoregressive U-Net (Ronneberger, Fischer, and Brox 2015): (i) raw data is processed by a small encoder network, (ii) then downsampled and passed through a main network operating on compressed chunks, (iii) and finally upsampled before being passed through a decoder network operating on the original resolution. This modularity creates a natural processing hierarchy where outer stages capture fine-grained patterns while inner stages operate on coarse representations akin to traditional tokens. Crucially, while the main network contains the bulk of parameters and can be any standard architecture designed for operating on tokenized language—such as a Transformer (Vaswani et al. 2017) or state space model (SSM) (Gu and Dao 2024)—we show that the encoder and decoder networks are strongly improved by using SSMs, which have an inductive bias for compression (Gu 2025). H-Net’s core is a novel dynamic chunking (DC) mechanism which interfaces between the main network and the encoder/decoder networks, learning how to segment data while using standard differentiable optimization. DC is composed of two complementary new techniques: (i) a routing module which predicts boundaries between adjacent elements through a similarity score (ii) and a smoothing module which interpolates representations using the router’s outputs, attenuating the effect of uncertain boundaries and significantly improving learnability. trace.question: How does H-Net perform dynamic chunking?
trace.answer:
**Dynamic Chunking in H‑Net**

H‑Net’s dynamic chunking (DC) is a learnable, end‑to‑end mechanism that decides where to split a raw sequence into chunks and how to compress those chunks for the main network.  
The DC layer is split into two complementary parts:

| Component | Function | How it works |
|-----------|----------|--------------|
| **Routing module** | Predicts chunk boundaries between adjacent elements | Computes a similarity‑based score for each pair of neighboring tokens; higher scores indicate a boundary. The scores are used to produce a binary boundary indicator (via a straight‑through estimator) that tells the downsampler which positions to keep. |
| **Downsampler** | Reduces sequence length | Keeps only the vectors at the predicted boundary positions, thereby compressing the sequence while preserving the most semantically important positions. |
| **Smoothing module** | Converts discrete chunks into continuous representations | Interpolates the representations across the boundaries predicted by the router, attenuating the effect of uncertain boundaries and improving learnability. |
| **Upsampler** | Restores the compressed representation to the original resolution | Uses the same boundary indicators to upsample the compressed vectors back to the original length for the decoder. |

Together, the routing and smoothing modules allow H‑Net to learn **data‑dependent, context‑aware segmentation** without any external supervision or heuristics. The routing module’s similarity scores are differentiable, and the smoothing module’s interpolation stabilises training, enabling the model to learn useful chunk boundaries that match the resolution of token‑based models (≈ 4.5–5 bytes per chunk) while remaining fully end‑to‑end.

trace.question: How does H-Net perform dynamic chunking?
trace.answer:
H‑Net learns how to split a long byte sequence into variable‑length chunks in a context‑dependent way.  
* The model first processes the raw bytes with an outer network (e.g., Mamba) that produces a representation for each byte.  
* A **dynamic chunking module** then decides, for each position, how many subsequent bytes should be grouped together. This decision is made by a learned soft‑gating mechanism that depends on the local context, rather than on a fixed width.  
* The chosen chunks are passed to an inner network that models the chunk‑level sequence.  
* H‑Net can stack this process in multiple stages: after the first stage the chunked sequence is again fed to another dynamic chunking module, allowing the model to learn a nested hierarchy of features.  

This data‑dependent, multi‑stage dynamic chunking is the first of its kind in byte‑level modeling and is shown to outperform static‑width heuristics and other hierarchical architectures.

trace.question: How does H-Net perform dynamic chunking?
trace.answer:
**Dynamic Chunking in H‑Net**

H‑Net’s dynamic chunking (DC) is a learnable, end‑to‑end mechanism that decides where to split a raw sequence into chunks and how to compress those chunks for the main network.  
The DC layer is split into two complementary sub‑modules:

| Sub‑module | Function | Key idea |
|------------|----------|----------|
| **Routing module** | Predicts a boundary score between every pair of adjacent elements in the input sequence. The score is a similarity measure that indicates whether the two elements should belong to the same chunk or to separate chunks. | The routing module is fully differentiable, so the boundary decisions can be optimized jointly with the rest of the model. |
| **Downsampler** | Uses the boundary scores to keep only the vectors that lie at the start of each predicted chunk, thereby reducing the sequence length while preserving the most semantically important positions. | The downsampler is a lightweight operation that directly follows the routing module. |
| **Smoothing module** | Converts the discrete chunk boundaries produced by the router into smooth, interpolated representations. It attenuates the effect of uncertain boundaries, which improves learnability and stability. | The smoothing module is applied in the de‑chunking (upsampling) stage, ensuring that the compressed representation can be reconstructed back to the original resolution. |
| **Upsampler** | Restores the compressed vectors to the original resolution using the boundary indicators. | Works together with the smoothing module to produce a full‑resolution output that can be fed to the decoder. |

These components are illustrated in Figure 1 of the paper, where the routing module and downsampler form the **chunking** side of a DC layer, and the smoothing module and upsampler form the **de‑chunking** side. The entire DC process is differentiable, allowing H‑Net to learn data‑dependent, context‑aware chunk boundaries without any external supervision or heuristics.

- Architectural illustration and component details: [2507.07955v2, PDF p. 3]

trace.question: How does H-Net learn where to place chunk boundaries?
trace.answer:
H‑Net learns where to place chunk boundaries by training a **routing module** that predicts a binary boundary indicator for every token in the sequence.  
During training the routing module is optimized jointly with the rest of the network, so the boundary decisions are learned end‑to‑end from the language‑model objective alone—no external supervision or heuristics are required. The routing module outputs a sequence of boundary indicators, which the downsampler then uses to keep only the vectors at the predicted boundaries, thereby reducing the sequence length while preserving semantically important positions. This dynamic, content‑dependent chunking is the core of H‑Net’s hierarchical design.

A Related Work The fundamental challenge of transforming raw sequential data into computationally efficient representations manifests across multiple domains through implicit chunking processes. In language modeling, this challenge is addressed through tokenization using static vocabularies derived from frequency-based algorithms such as Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) (Sennrich, Haddow, and Birch 2015) in GPT models (Radford et al. 2019; Brown et al. 2020) and SentencePiece (Kudo and Richardson 2018) in Llama architectures (Touvron, Martin, et al. 2023; Grattafiori et al. 2024). Computer vision addresses similar challenges through spatial pooling operations (Ronneberger, Fischer, and Brox 2015) that aggregate neighboring pixels into meaningful representations. Despite achieving strong empirical performance, it is widely known that traditional tokenization approaches in language models suffer from fundamental limitations that constrain model capabilities. Fixed vocabularies exhibit biases toward high- resource languages, demonstrate fragility when handling adversarial inputs, and show lower performance on character-level tasks (Petrov et al. 2023; Ahia, Kumar, Gonen, Kasai, et al. 2023; Belinkov and Bisk 2017; Sun et al. 2020; Xue et al. 2022). These limitations stem from the static nature of predefined vocabularies, which cannot adapt their chunking strategies to input content or context. To address these constraints, tokenizer-free methods have emerged that avoid the reliance on predefined vocabularies. • In Appendix A.1, we discuss the most directly related prior work on autoregressive sequence models, extending the overview from Section 1. • In Appendix A.2, we discuss non-autoregressive models. However, we provide this delineation because it marks an important difference in motivation that influences design considerations and downstream evaluations. • Appendix A.3 mentions other works in non-language modalities related to tokenization. Hierarchical architectures with external chunking strategeies, where chunk boundaries are provided by an external function or module. 4. Hierarchical architectures with dynamic chunking strategies, where chunk boundaries are content-dependent and learned end-to-end. Since this naive approach suffers from computational challenges on long sequences, Mam- baByte (Wang et al. 2024) proposed using a state space model for its linear-time efficiency. We similarly use Mamba(-2) (Dao and Gu 2024) layers in the outer stages of an H-Net. trace.question: How does H-Net learn where to place chunk boundaries?
trace.answer:
H‑Net learns chunk boundaries end‑to‑end by using a **routing module** that predicts a binary boundary indicator for every adjacent pair of tokens.  
The router computes a similarity score between neighboring representations; a threshold (implemented with a straight‑through estimator) turns this score into a hard boundary decision.  
These hard decisions are then used by the **downsampler** to keep only the vectors that lie at the start of a chunk, thereby reducing the sequence length.  
Because the router’s outputs are differentiable through the straight‑through estimator and the whole system is trained with a standard loss (plus an auxiliary down‑sampling‑ratio loss), the model learns to place boundaries that best preserve the information needed for the downstream task.

trace.question: How does H-Net learn where to place chunk boundaries?
trace.answer:
H‑Net learns chunk boundaries end‑to‑end by using a **routing module** that predicts a binary boundary indicator for every adjacent pair of input tokens.  
The routing module computes a similarity score between neighboring representations; a threshold (or a learned gating function) turns this score into a hard boundary decision.  
These boundary predictions are then used by the **downsampler** to keep only the vectors that lie at the start of a chunk, thereby reducing the sequence length.  
The whole process is trained jointly with the rest of the model using a combination of:

* a **routing loss** that encourages the desired down‑sampling ratio,  
* a **smoothing module** that interpolates across uncertain boundaries to stabilize gradients, and  
* gradient‑based learning of discrete choices via straight‑through estimators (Fedus, Zoph, and Shazeer 2022; Bengio, Léonard, and Courville 2013).

Thus, H‑Net learns where to place chunk boundaries purely from the task loss, without any external tokenizer or heuristic.

trace.question: What is the purpose of the routing module in H-Net?
trace.answer:
The routing module in H‑Net is responsible for **dynamically determining where chunk boundaries should be placed**.  
It computes a probability \(p_t\) (using a scaled‑cosine similarity between the current token’s key and the previous key) that indicates whether the current token should start a new chunk. This decision is then used by the downsampler to decide which token representations are retained for the next, coarser‑level processing, thereby controlling the sequence length and the amount of compute applied to each token.

In its simplest form, a single-stage H-Net consists of one encoder network, one main network, and one decoder network. Crucially, the architecture’s key characteristic lies in the main network’s unique property: it can itself be instantiated as a complete H-Net, enabling recursive construction of multi-level hierarchies. This recursive design allows H-Net to scale to arbitrary depths. In an 𝑆-stage model, we denote components at each stage using superscripts: encoder networks as E𝑠and decoder networks as D𝑠for stages 0 ≤𝑠< 𝑆, with the main network M residing only at the final stage 𝑠= 𝑆. For example, a two-stage model contains E0, E1, M, D1, and D0, as illustrated 4Chunking is a formal concept from cognitive psychology central to human memory and cognition, and is the inspiration for this work’s terminology. 5https://github.com/goombalab/hnet 6https://huggingface.co/cartesia-ai 4

in Figure 1-(Left). Throughout this paper, we use superscripts to denote stage indices, though we omit them when all variables within an equation belong to the same stage. Drawing inspiration from the U-Net architecture (Ronneberger, Fischer, and Brox 2015), H-Net progressively compresses input sequences into fewer vectors with richer semantic embeddings through a chunking layer, processes these representa- tions in the main network, then decompresses the sequence back to its original resolution using a dechunking layer. Unlike traditional U-Net designs, however, H-Net dynamically determines chunking boundaries rather than using fixed-size pooling operations. The overall pipeline can be formalized as: ˆ𝑥𝑠= E𝑠(𝑥𝑠), ˆ𝑧𝑆= M(𝑥𝑆), ˆ𝑧𝑠= D𝑠(𝑧𝑠), (1) where the chunking layer and the dechunking layer operations are defined as: (𝑥𝑠+1, 𝑝𝑠) = Chunk( ˆ𝑥𝑠), (2) 𝑧𝑠= Dechunk(ˆ𝑧𝑠+1, 𝑝𝑠) + Linear( ˆ𝑥𝑠). (3) The initial input to the model is 𝑥0 ∈R𝐿0×𝐷0 where 𝐿0 is the input sequence length and 𝐷0 is the embedding dimension. **Encoder**  
- Compresses the uncompressed input sequence into a smaller set of “chunked” vectors that carry richer semantic information for the main network.  
- At the same time it must preserve fine‑grained details so that these can be recovered by the corresponding decoder through residual connections.  
- The encoder therefore serves a dual purpose: (i) dimensionality reduction for efficient processing in later stages, and (ii) a conduit for passing high‑resolution information to the decoder.  
- It operates on the full, uncompressed sequence, so its design is constrained by computational efficiency.  
- In the final H‑Net configuration the encoder is built from Mamba‑2 layers, which are well‑suited to handling fine‑grained data and to compressing information into fixed‑size states.  
  [2507.07955v2, PDF p. 5]  
  [2507.07955v2, PDF p. 19]

**Main network**  
- Receives the compressed representation produced by the encoder (after the chunking operation).  
- Because the sequence length has been reduced, the main network can afford more parameters and compute per token, allowing it to learn higher‑level abstractions.  
- It functions as a standard language model (e.g., a Transformer or other sequence‑mixing architecture) and is the core of the hierarchical hierarchy.  
- The main network is the only component that is present at the final stage of a multi‑stage H‑Net; earlier stages contain only encoders and decoders.  
  [2507.07955v2, PDF p. 5]  
  [2507.07955v2, PDF p. 4]

**Decoder**  
- Takes the output of the main network (the compressed, high‑level representation) and “dechunk”‑s it back to the original sequence resolution.  
- It combines the coarse‑grained information from the main network with the fine‑grained residuals supplied by the encoder.  
- Like the encoder, the decoder processes the uncompressed sequence, so its design must also be computationally efficient.  
- In the final H‑Net architecture the decoder is also implemented with Mamba‑2 layers, matching the encoder’s compression‑oriented design.

Evaluation protocol. For each model, we measure the proportion of generations (out of 100,000) that reproduce the most frequent audio segment detected in our whole training dataset. For this purpose, we have first developed a matching system that detects the most frequent audio segments, see Appendix B. We select the most frequent one that is long enough (16 seconds) and easy to detect from text and audio. We measure the proportion of generations that exactly match this most frequent segment. For the matching, we initially use both audio and text matching, but observe that text-based matching has a higher recall for the initial matching step. We manually verify all the generations to filter out outliers that are not exact matches. Unconditioned and prompted generation: We first measure what happens with unconditional generation, to evaluate whether the model tends to generate specific sequences when not guided by a prompt. Characterizing Audio Artifacts Caused by Quantization First, recall that Moshi jointly outputs two streams of tokens, Wk for text, and As,k for audio, where 1 ≤k ≤Q corresponds to the semantic+acoustic tokens of Moshi, while Q + 1 ≤k ≤2Q are the tokens predicting the other speaker’s voice. We first compute the Shannon entropy H across windows of fixed size C at each timestep i for each of this stream independently. This yields H0i = H(W[i−C:i]) for text, and Hki = H(A[i−C:i],k) for audio. Note that we only consider the stream of Moshi (k ≤Q). We use C = 64 in practice, which corresponds to roughly 4.5 seconds of audio once decoded, and ignore all the leading C tokens as they have a shorted context (and include the prompt used for generation). We observe qualitatively that the entropy spectrum is often indicative of artifacts or degradations of the audio samples. Formally we define three types of artifacts from the entropy statistics, as described below. In practice, we characterize the presence or absence of each artifact over non-overlapping windows of ω = 64 tokens, as illustrated in Figure 10. Repetitive text A first observed degradation is the model quickly repeating short sen- tences or words. This characterized by the text entropy being almost flat over a window H0i:i+ω, but non zero (as more than one token is repeated), as seen in Figure 10 (c). We measure the “flatness” of H0i:i+ω by fitting a linear regression model to it and verifying whether the slope is below a certain threshold hyperparameter ηflat = 1e−3. Silence vs Background Noise By design, Moshi being silent corresponds to a constant stream of PAD text tokens (hence H0i:i+ω = 0), while simultaneously, the corresponding audio tokens decode to a near silent waveform: The audio tokens are not constant, but fall into a small subset of “silence tokens”, which results in a lower overall entropy for the audio tokens as seen for instance in the short silences of Figure 10 (a). We measure this behavior as mediank>1,i(Hki:i+ω) ≤ηaudio silence = 2. Note that we do not consider these silences to be artifacts: This is because silences occur naturally in the multistream model as they simply represent the other speaker’s turn. For illustration purposes, we highlight silences throughout Figure 6 and 10, but we count them as artifact-free timesteps otherwise. In contrast, background noise artifacts occur when the text stream is silent (H0i:i+ω = 0), but audio tokens still have a rich output (mediank>1,i(Hki:i+ω) > ηaudio silence). This is shown in Figure 10 (d) where a silence slowly degrades into background noise over time. Bad audio quality The last category of artifacts encompasses degraded audio quality while the main speaker (Moshi) is speaking: • Gibberish is a very common type of artifacts at low bitwidth quantization (W2) and corresponds to incoherent speech. Finally, we set the speaker identity for the first speaker stream to be that of Moshi, a useful conversational assistant, with a final stage of instruct finetuning. We use the synthetic instruct dataset described in Section 4.3, with a batch size of 2.7 hours of audio, for 30k steps, with a learning rate of 2 · 10−6 for both transformers. During this stage, we also perform data augmentation on the stream corresponding to the user in order to make Moshi more robust to various situations. Namely, we apply a random gain to the user stream between -24 dB and +15 dB, 50% of the time. 30% of the time, we further add noise extracts from the Deep Noise Suppression challenge (Dubey et al., 2023) which we concatenate in order to cover the entire duration of each training example. The noise is amplified to reach a target volume relative to the original source between -30 dB and +6 dB. Each time we need to sample a new noise, we alternatively use a silent section with a random duration up to 30 seconds of silence with probability of 50%, so that the model can handle the audio condition going from noisy to silent, and vice versa. We emulate echo from Moshi into the user’s microphone by adding a scaled down copy of Moshi’s stream into the user’s stream, scaled by as factor uniformly sampled in [0, 0.2], and a delay uniformly sampled between [100ms, 500ms]. Finally, we apply to the user’s stream, potentially augmented with the echo, a reverb-like augmentation as introduced by Defossez et al. (2020). In addition, we systematically control the data and compute budget for all models (see Table 1), matching all models carefully in both bytes-per-batch and FLOPs-per-byte:13 • Data Budget: We train all models on the 100B token subset sampled from the FineWeb-Edu dataset (Penedo et al. 2024). All tokenizer-free models process 8192 utf-8 encoded bytes per sequence, while the Transformer uses 1792 tokens from the GPT2 tokenizer (roughly equivalent to 8192 bytes). We use batch size 256 for all models; the total batch size is just under 0.5M tokens per batch for the baseline BPE Transformer, roughly matching protocols from prior work (Gu and Dao 2024). • Compute Budget: For calculating FLOPs, we follow standard methodology (Hoffmann et al. 2022) with an extension for Mamba-2 layers (see Appendix B). We use the BPE-tokenized Transformer’s #FLOPs as a reference, and the number of layers of the other models is adjusted accordingly to match the reference #FLOPs.
